en: Following the exposition of reality (*tattva*), the cultivation of the counteragent (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), its stages, and the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*) must be explained.
Therefore, the fourth chapter is commenced for the purpose of explaining those.
Since they were mentioned immediately after reality, and because the stages and the attainment of the fruit are dependent upon the cultivation of the counteragent, their enumeration follows.

Demonstrating that the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) are intended in the Sūtra as being the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), he says: "The cultivation of the antidotes is the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
For when they are cultivated for the sake of abandoning the aforementioned obstructions and their opposites, they become effective; thus they are called "antidotes.
Furthermore, these are thirty-seven, ranging from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Their synonyms are cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇā*), application (*āropaṇā*), practice (*abhyāsa*), and frequent repetition (*bahulīkriyā*). This [cultivation] must now be explained, as it was indicated immediately after the [four] realities (*tattva*).

For what reason is the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) alone mentioned first, and not the other cultivations of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)? It is said: "In that regard, first of all, because of the grossness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and because of being the cause of craving (*tarṣa*)," and so forth.
"In that regard" means in the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence;
first, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is explained, and afterwards those of the others as well.

Because they do not understand the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, fools—due to their clinging to conditioned phenomena as pleasant, pure, permanent, and self—rejoice in the enjoyments of existence and feel terror toward nirvāṇa.

That lack of understanding regarding virtues and faults, as well as the clinging to pleasure and so forth, is turned away by the vision of the truths; therefore, for the sake of inducing revulsion toward saṃsāra and for the sake of turning one toward nirvāṇa, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is taught at the very beginning for the purpose of entering the four truths.
For it is by means of the body that *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption) is manifested; thus, *dauṣṭhulya* is a state of instability.
For in this way, the body is indeed subject to transformation as it is conditioned day after day; therefore, *dauṣṭhulya* is manifested through the body.
And consequently, by means of the investigation of the body, one enters into the Truth of Suffering.
What is the reason? Because its characteristic is conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Since the characteristic—that is, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—of the truth of suffering consists of conditioned phenomena accompanied by functional rigidity, and since functional rigidity is manifested through the body, one enters into the truth of suffering by means of examining the body.
Because functional rigidity is not understood, he says: "For functional rigidity is the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)."
The conditioning of phenomena is their arising;
and because it is the basis for all calamities, it is *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption);
and because it is contrary to the Noble Ones, it is suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
As it has been said:
"This birth is a misfortune, for when there is birth, there exist enemies such as old age, death, disease, calamity, slaughter, and bondage.
Those misfortunes would not exist if there were no arising of manifold fears; just as when a tree has not yet grown, there is indeed no falling [of its branches] by wind or fire."

"By that" means by way of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and not by way of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) or the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because those two do not pervade [all things] and because they have the suffering of conditioned formations as their cause.
Noble ones perceive every contaminated (*sāsrava*) entity as suffering, but not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) entities, because the Truth of the Path is the antidote to the arising of birth.
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), however, do not perceive them so, because their intentions are impaired by cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*).
It is also said in the Sūtra: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Others say that the state of unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) is the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Still others maintain that it is not unserviceability, but rather corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*), that constitutes it.
What is the reason? Because it is unserviceable due to being *sāsrava* (with-outflows), that which is *sāsrava* must necessarily be admitted to have seeds as its cause.
Yet, even though it lacks seeds, such [unserviceability] sometimes occurs within the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of an Arhat due to the improper consumption of food and so forth.
And this cannot be considered *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption), because it is *anāsrava* (without-outflows).
Therefore, the seed of the *sāsrava* (contaminated) dharmas residing in the *ālayavijñāna* is here intended as *dauṣṭhulya* (disquiet).
This body, accompanied by pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure, is its fruit.
Consequently, that *dauṣṭhulya* is manifested—that is, made known—by the body which arises moment by moment and is accompanied by states such as pleasure.
It is just as a seed within a granary hole [is known] by its sprout.
Therefore, one enters into the Truth of Suffering through the examination of the body.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because it has the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) accompanied by functional rigidity (dauṣṭhulya)," which means that its nature consists of conditioned phenomena together with their seeds.

The suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is indeed called "dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya*) because it is accompanied by both the dysfunction of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the dysfunction of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), and because it is their cause.
For this very reason, through the suffering inherent in conditioned formations, the Noble Ones perceive every contaminated thing as suffering.
In this way, one enters into the Truth of Suffering by means of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Feeling is the cause of craving, because it is intended [here] as that which arises from contact associated with ignorance; for feeling that is untainted (anāsrava) is not such a cause.
In this context, pleasant feeling is the cause of craving for union with and non-separation from it;
painful feeling is the cause of craving for non-union with and separation from it.

The state of neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] is the cause for the craving for delight in that state and for the craving for union with and non-separation from it in certain meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Because of the statement, "Touched by painful feeling, one relishes sensual pleasure," even painful feeling becomes a cause for craving for pleasure.
Through the investigation of that, one enters into the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*).
For he, examining sensation (*vedanā*) by way of its intrinsic nature, its cause, its impermanence, and its suffering, enters into the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*).
The meaning is that he understands craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its effect.
For in the Sūtra, craving is stated to be the truth of the origin.
What is the origin of suffering? It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion; such is the detailed explanation.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to feeling, one enters into the truth of the origin [of suffering].
The mind is the basis for the adherence to a self.
Since there is no other self (*ātman*) characterized by qualities such as permanence, the mind itself is the objective support for the clinging to a self.
Therefore, through the investigation of that [mind], one enters into the Truth of Cessation as being peaceful.
He states the reason for this very point: "because of the disappearance of the fear of the annihilation of the self."
For when the mind is examined for its impermanence and other characteristics, the adherence to a self is turned away and the perception of suffering arises.
Consequently, through the disappearance of the fear of the annihilation of a self, one enters into the truth of cessation as peace, because it is merely the cessation of suffering.
Thus, one enters into the truth of cessation by means of the application of mindfulness to the mind.

Through the investigation of phenomena (*dharmaparīkṣā*), one enters into the truth of the path by means of non-delusion regarding phenomena that are defiling and those that are purifying. In this context, defiling phenomena are the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Purifying phenomena are those that serve as the antidotes to the secondary afflictions, such as the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Having understood the relationship between the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) among those things that are defiled (*sāṃkleśika*) and those that are purifying (*vyāvadānika*), one becomes oriented toward the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), which is the means for the absolute abandonment of all calamities.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the truth of the path.
Here, "entry" (*avatāra*) refers to the realization of the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of each individual truth.

In that regard, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body is [to be practiced] by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; also by way of its nature as consisting of many impure substances, its impure seed, its impure outflow, its cause for the persistence of impurity, its transformation into impurity, its lack of essence like a mass of foam, and also by way of its destination and its mode of birth.

Furthermore, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena is undertaken by way of the impermanent, the suffering, the empty, and the non-self; by way of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), causes, results, realms, stages, and levels; by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; and by way of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

For Bodhisattvas, however, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness is likewise performed in the mode of non-apprehension (*anupalambhākāra*) for the purpose of abandoning conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Although the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have wisdom (prajñā) as their intrinsic nature, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" because they are established through the power of mindfulness; that is, mindfulness is established by means of them, thus they are "foundations of mindfulness.
Immediately after the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, the cultivation of the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) is taught.
For what reason? To this he says: "Because when the adverse factors (vipakṣa) have been fully understood," and so forth.

Although it is stated without qualification as "by the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthānabhāvanayā*), it should be understood specifically as the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

This is because, through aspects such as the elements (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as well as by way of the distinctions between the contaminated and uncontaminated realms, the stages, and those in training and those beyond training, both the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are thoroughly known in every respect; thus, there is the removal of the adverse factors.
Here, the removal of the adverse factors consists in the severance of the continuity of those already arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen.

And for the sake of approaching the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), there is the arrival of the counteragent, which consists in the continuation of the series of those [counteragents] already arisen and the production of those not yet arisen. "Vigor (*vīrya*) operates in four ways" means that the operation of vigor is fourfold, based on the distinction between the adverse side (*vipakṣa*) and the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), and between those already arisen and those not yet arisen.
By this scriptural passage—"for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen," and so forth—he demonstrates that vigor itself functions in four ways.
By the mention of "and so forth" (*vistara*), there is a connection to the remainder of the text.
In that regard, the remaining text is as follows: "He generates desire for abandonment, exerts himself, arouses vigor, upholds the mind, and correctly applies himself."
Thus, one generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states; this is the detailed explanation.
Thus, one generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; this is the detailed explanation.
One generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and correctly applies oneself for the stability, increase, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.
The stability of those that have arisen is non-decline;
their increase is production in a continuous succession;
their fulfillment is the reaching of excellence.
"He generates desire" indicates the application of the cultivation of respectful vigor.
"He exerts himself" means that he directs his body and mind toward the abandonment of laziness.
"He initiates vigor" is for the purpose of removing lethargy and restlessness.
How does one initiate [the effort]? One uplifts the sunken mind through mental attentions toward phenomena that inspire a sense of urgency (*saṃvejana*) and joy (*pramodana*).
One correctly applies the agitated mind to that very same object; the meaning is that one sustains it through mental attentions toward phenomena that inspire a sense of urgency and joy.
In this way, it is made known that the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) consist of the nature of vigor (*vīrya*).
They are called the "right efforts" (*samyakpradhāna*) because by means of them one correctly sustains body, speech, and mind.
"Adaptability (*karmanyatā*) therein for stability," and so forth;
"therein" refers to that cultivation of vigor which consists in the removal of opposing factors and the acquisition of their antidotes.

Workability (*karmaṇyatā*) is the fitness of the mind’s stability for the successful accomplishment of all aims. And that workability arises through the predominance of desire, energy, mind, and investigation; therefore, it is said: "Workability is the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The "success" (*ṛddhi*) is the accomplishment of every aim, such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth.

They are called "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*) because they serve as the foundation for that [psychic power]; the meaning is that they are the causes of psychic power. For this very reason, it is said: "because they are the cause for the successful accomplishment of all goals. Furthermore, these are: the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment.

In that regard, concentration of aspiration (*chanda-samādhi*) is when, through the predominance of aspiration, one applies oneself with reverence to the exertion of vigor and touches one-pointedness of mind.
Concentration of vigor (*vīrya-samādhi*) is when, while exerting vigor, one touches one-pointedness of mind through continuous application.
Concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*) is when, having recourse to the seed of prior concentration, one touches one-pointedness of mind by holding the mind within the mind itself.
The meditative concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*) is that which, having investigated the object of focus, touches upon one-pointedness of mind.
Here, "abiding" refers to the abiding of the mind; it should be understood as meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The inclusion of the term "concentration" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

Since the adaptability of the mind (*cittakarmaṇyatā*) belongs to one who has initiated vigor, and this consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the bases of psychic power are taught immediately after the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Furthermore, for what purpose and with what cause does that adaptability exist? To this he says: "It should be understood as following from the cultivation of the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) for the sake of abandoning the five faults.
Here, "following" (*anvaya*) means "cause" (*hetu*).
And since those five faults are not understood, he asks: "Which are the five faults? Showing them, he says: "Laziness, forgetting the instruction, lethargy, and agitation," and so forth in detail.
Since these are indeed six faults, he says: "In that context, lethargy and agitation are treated as a single fault."
Therefore, there are five [faults].
Among them, laziness is a fault at the time of application because of the resulting lack of application;
for one who has applied himself, the loss of instruction is a fault because of the consequent absence of mental concentration.
For one who is concentrated, lethargy and excitement are defects because they prevent the mind's adaptability (*cittakarmaṇyatā*).
During the state of lethargy and excitement, non-application (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is a defect;
non-application here refers to equanimity (*upekṣā*), and by means of it, those two [defects] are not pacified.
Volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*) pertains to tranquility (*praśānti*); "fault" (*doṣa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Volitional effort is volition (*cetanā*).
For it is called "tranquil" because, through the disappearance of lethargy and excitement, equanimity has been attained.
The formative forces for abandonment are the "abandonment-formative forces" (*prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*).
For the abandonment of what? For the abandonment of the five faults just mentioned.
If this is so, then it must be explained: how are eight abandonment-formative forces established for the abandonment of these [faults]?

In that regard, there are four factors for the abandonment of laziness: zeal, exertion, faith, and pliancy. Among these, zeal is aspiration; exertion is vigor; faith is deep conviction; and pliancy is serviceability.
How, then, are these established as being for the abandonment of laziness? To this he says: "Furthermore, they should be understood in their proper order."
"The basis, that which is based upon it, its cause, and its fruit. Thus, he shows that because these are mutually influenced, they lead to the abandonment of laziness.
Desire is the basis of exertion;
exertion is that which is based upon it, because desire precedes exertion.
Faith is the cause of that basis, which is desire.
How so? To this he says: "Because of desire [for action] when there is conviction.
For one who has faith, there arises a desire for action regarding the cause and its fruit.
The fruit of that exertion which is based upon it is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
How so? To this he says: "Because one who has initiated vigor attains a specific state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
For the attainment of a specific state of meditative concentration is the cause of pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
Therefore, it is said that for one who has initiated vigor, pliancy is the fruit of exertion, because of the attainment of a specific state of meditative concentration.
For thus, in one who has initiated vigor, joy arises through the departure from the impurities of coarseness, discursive thought, and so forth.
In one whose mind is joyful, there is pliancy of body and mind, characterized by functional flexibility (*karmanyatā*).
From that, there occurs the attainment of a distinguished state of concentration (*samādhi*).
And here, vigor is described as having both a cause and a fruit by way of being the antidote to laziness.

It is stated that these are the antidotes to the four faults respectively: therein, mindfulness is the antidote to forgetting the instruction; clear comprehension is the antidote to lethargy and excitement; volition is the antidote to non-application; and equanimity is the antidote to application. Here, "equanimity of formations" is to be understood as [the equanimity] regarding mental formations.

Furthermore, with the intention of explaining the characteristics of mindfulness and the others, he says this: "Moreover, those [factors] beginning with mindfulness are to be understood in their respective order.
The detailed explanation is: "Mindfulness is the non-forgetting of the object. This means that mindfulness is the verbal expression of the basis for the instruction on mental stability.
Clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) is the awareness of laxity and excitement when there is no loss of mindfulness (*smṛtyasaṃpramoṣa*).
For one whose mindfulness is established necessarily possesses clear comprehension; therefore, he says: "when there is no loss of mindfulness.
The meaning is that, having recognized laxity and excitement, [the mind] proceeds effortlessly because it moves in the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
"Equanimity" means the non-formation of mental activity toward other objects.
This is what is meant: one whose mindfulness is well-established understands, as it truly is, whether the mind is sunken or excited during instruction;
and for the sake of removing that sinking and excitement, one applies formative effort.
"And one is equanimous upon the disappearance of lethargy and excitement.
Thus, there is for him pliancy (*praśaṭhatā*) and serviceability (*karmanyatā*) of the mind.

And here, in the term "stability of serviceability" (*karmanyatā-sthiti*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in the case of "hardness" (*khakkhaṭatva*) and so forth.
It is connected that immediately after the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*) beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) were taught.
The intention [of the question] is: "How are they established? By what meaning?
Therefore, he says: "When the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been planted, by virtue of the predominance of zeal (*chanda*) and application (*yoga*)," and so forth.

The phrase "by way of predominance" (ādhipatyataḥ) continues [from the previous context]. By this, he shows that the word "predominance" (ādhipatya), employed in the expression "by way of the predominance of the application of desire" (chanda-yoga-ādhipatyataḥ), carries over into what follows as well.

When the roots of merit conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) are established in one whose mind has become pliant through the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the roots of merit conducive to liberation find their footing within the mental continuum of that pliant mind.
This occurs by way of the predominance of desire, up to the predominance of investigation; however, it does not occur for one whose mind is not pliant.
And that pliancy of mind arises through the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Therefore, immediately after the bases of psychic power, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are established on account of their predominance in planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

Regarding the phrase "by the predominance of desire" (*chandādhipatyataḥ*), faith itself is expressed here by the word "desire" through a metaphorical application of the effect to the cause, just as one says "curd-clover" or "instant-fever."

Alternatively, the definition of *śraddhā* (faith) consists respectively in conviction (*abhisaṃpratyaya*), clarity (*prasāda*), and aspiration (*abhilāṣa*) regarding existence, excellence, and capability.
Therefore, by the mention of "desire" (*cchanda*) here, it is *śraddhā* characterized by aspiration that is intended, and not mere desire.
Regarding the phrase "by the predominance of application" (*prayogādhipatyataḥ*): "application" (*prayoga*) is so called because one applies oneself by means of it.

By the word "application" (prayoga), vigor (vīrya) is intended. "Through the sovereignty of non-forgetfulness regarding the object" means through the sovereignty of the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya).
The faculty of mindfulness has the characteristic of verbalizing the object.
"By way of the sovereignty of non-diffusion" means by way of the sovereignty of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
For non-diffusion is indeed the faculty of concentration, because its characteristic is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
And "by way of the sovereignty of discernment" means by way of the sovereignty of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Because the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) has the nature of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*),

the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) should be understood as being [the faculties] respectively, by virtue of their sovereignty in planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
For one who possesses faith exerts vigor (*vīrya*) for the sake of escaping from the prison of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
For one who has initiated vigor, the three trainings are accomplished:
the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, respectively.
Thus, on the stage of application for the path of seeing, the predominance of the faculties is maintained.

Others, however, say: the status of faith and the other [faculties] as faculties does not arise from their sovereignty over the planting of the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

What then? Once the roots of merit conducive to liberation have been planted, these are called "faculties" because of the sovereignty of aspiration (*chanda*) and the others. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The status of faith as a faculty [arises] from the sovereignty of aspiration"—this is how it is connected.
"Application" (*prayoga*) means activity (*vyāpāra*).
Non-forgetfulness is the non-loss of the focal object;
non-diffusion is the absence of distraction;
discernment is thorough investigation.

Due to their predominance over application, non-confusion, non-distraction, and discernment, the mental factors termed energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) receive the designation of "faculties" (*indriya*).

However, this must be addressed here: once the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been planted, there is no specific excellence of self-nature in faith and the others that distinguishes the state of having planted them from the state prior to it.
For it is precisely because of their predominance in that state that they are established as faculties.
